panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Longitudinal axial MRI images of a human patient showing progression of brain abnormalities consistent with the case report on pontocerebellar hypoplasia. B: Axial T2-weighted image showing characteristic 'figure of 8' midbrain appearance and small basal ganglia, supporting the diagnosis of pontocerebellar hypoplasia. C: Axial T2-weighted image included to demonstrate characteristic brain abnormalities in the context of pontocerebellar hypoplasia. D: Coronal T2-FLAIR image showing hypoplasia and atrophy of the cerebellar hemispheres with vermis sparing, a key finding in pontocerebellar hypoplasia. E: Sagittal T1-weighted image demonstrating a small pons and thinning of the corpus callosum, characteristic findings of pontocerebellar hypoplasia.

panels.figure_caption: Coronal (A) and axial (B) T2-weighted images show global cerebellar hypoplasia with symmetric involvement of both hemispheres and vermis, along with a very large cisterna magna. There was no obvious abnormality of the brainstem. The cerebellar folia and fourth ventricle were not dilated, indicating there was no volume loss. The cerebellar foliation pattern was normal and there were no heterotopic nodules of gray matter, indicating there was no dysplasia.
in_text_mentions: Absence of neurological improvement prompted extended metabolic and endocrine evaluations: the levels of serum amino acids, sialotransferrin, TSH, free T4, cortisol, ammonia, and 17 OH progesterone were found to be within normal range. Urine amino acid analysis detected mild elevation (11 mmol/mol creatinine) in excretion of 3-methylglutaconic acid, implying possible mitochondrial dysfunction (14). Brain MRI on day 6 showed cerebellar hypoplasia with symmetric involvement of the vermis and hemispheres, without dysplasia (Figure 1) and a potential ischemic thalamic lesion (Figure 2).

Inborn error of metabolism was initially excluded by normal levels of serum ammonia, serum lactate, plasma amino acids and urine organic acids. Chromosomal analysis demonstrated a normal female karyotype (46, XX). Brain MRI performed at 1 year of age revealed a small brainstem, hypoplastic vermis, bilateral hippocampal atrophy, and reduced cerebellar hemispheres with widened choroid fissures (Figures 1(a) and 1(b)). The corpus callosum appeared thin, and diffuse cerebral atrophy was noted.

atrophy, and severe developmental delay [2]. Our patient's early-onset, refractory seizures at 2 months and global developmental delay align with previous reports [6]. Brain MRI findings in PCH3 typically show severe cerebellar hypoplasia, particularly in the vermis, significant pontine hypoplasia with flattened ventral pons, and a thin corpus callosum. Compared to PCH1 and PCH2, cerebellar and pontine hypoplasia in PCH3 is less extreme [9]. In addition to the classical clinical features of PCH3, all the characteristic brain MRI findings in PCH3 were also identified in our patient (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Sagittal T1-weighted image showing reduced size of the cerebellum and pons, and hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, confirming the diagnosis of Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia as stated in the title and caption. B: Axial T2-weighted image demonstrating significant white matter loss, a common finding in cerebral hypoplasia associated with the specified disease. C: Axial T2-weighted image demonstrating pontine atrophy, which is a feature consistent with brainstem hypoplasia in Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia.

At one month of age, a simple cranial computed tomography scan was performed due to a pinpoint fontanelle and hypotonia, revealing hypoplasia of the corpus callosum (not shown). Subsequently, cerebral magnetic resonance imaging was performed, revealing colpocephaly indicative of white matter loss, resembling a periventricular leukomalacia, and resulting in a significant reduction in the size of the corpus callosum. The imaging also revealed hypoplasia of the brainstem and cerebellar structures (Figure 1).

MRI controlled at the age of 3 months and 20 months showed progressive pontine and vermis atrophy (Figure 1B,C) as well cerebellar hemisphere atrophy (Figure 1G,K), persistent delayed myelination, and progressive thalami atrophy (Figure 1K,L,M).

tongue fasciculation was noted in one patient. MRI showed cerebellar atrophy in almost all cases (9/9) and vermis atrophy was reported in six patients. Of note, a longitudinal MRI study performed in our patient at 2 weeks, 3 months and 1 year 8 months demonstrated the progressive course of cerebral atrophy, cerebellar atrophy, and white matter atrophy in the supratentorial area and demyelination (Figure 1). EMG showed motor neuronopathy. Three of the reported patients died at 10 years (patient 7), 2 years (patient 10, this study) and 1.5 years (patient 2) (Figure 2 and Supplementary Table S1).

findings.label: Cerebellar vermis hypoplasia
findings.evidence: Large cisterna magna and cerebellar hypoplasia with the majority of the cerebellar vermis can be seen

panels.rationale: The figure is a T1-weighted brain MRI of a newborn showing extensive cerebellar hypoplasia and a large cisterna magna. This presentation is consistent with the defined disease, Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia, specifically manifesting as cerebellar vermis hypoplasia.

panels.figure_caption: T1-blade sag on day two of life. Large cisterna magna and cerebellar hypoplasia with the majority of the cerebellar vermis can be seen, suggesting a possible Dandy-Walker variant (cerebellar vermis hypoplasia).
in_text_mentions: brain MRI showed a large cisterna magna and cerebellar hypoplasia with the majority of the cerebellar vermis present, suggesting a possible Dandy-Walker variant (cerebellar vermis hypoplasia) (Figure 1). Pediatric Neurology recommended chromosomal microarray which was normal. At three months, an echocardiogram was performed due to a new systolic murmur and showed a moderate-to-large atrial septal defect with bilateral atrial dilation, but normal ventricular function.
